newsitem.title: FRANCE: European rights court deals double blow to Turkey.
newsitem.headline: European rights court deals double blow to Turkey.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights dealt a double blow to Turkey on Wednesday, ruling that Ankara had violated the rights of a Greek Cypriot with land in northern Cyprus and tortured a suspected Kurdish guerrilla.
Turkish authorities had no immediate comment, but the rulings in widely-watched cases seemed bound to bolster already widespread criticism of Ankara's human rights record.

In a landmark finding, the court rejected Turkey's argument that the European human rights convention did not apply to its occupation of the north of Cyprus since it occurred before Ankara accepted its jurisdiction.

Cypriot lawyers said the ruling was significant because it made Turkey responsible for the situation on the island rather than the breakaway Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus declared in 1983 and recognised only by Ankara.

"I believe its effects can be enormous," Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides told reporters following the judgment. "If we take into account those who were forced to leave their homes then the effects can be greater."
About 200,000 Greek Cypriots were displaced when Turkish troops took control of the northern third of Cyprus in 1974 after a brief coup engineered by a military junta then ruling Greece.
The court upheld a complaint by tourist guide Titina Loizidou that Turkey violated her property rights by denying her access to land she owned in Kyrenia, northern Cyprus.
It found by a vote of 11-6 that the Turkish army "exercised effective overall control" in Cyprus.
Loizidou told reporters she was sure the judgment would help the search for a solution to the Cyprus problem.

"This is an historic decision. It is the first time an international court has taken a legal decision on Turkey's responsibility in northern Cyprus and found Turkey guilty for denying people the right to enjoy their property," she said.

In the second case, the court, an arm of the 40-nation Council of Europe that promotes human rights and democracy, ruled that Turkish police tortured a Kurd, Zeki Aksoy, in 1992 after arresting him as a suspected terrorist.
Ankara was ordered to pay 4.3 billion Turkish lire ($41,000) in damages plus legal fees of 20,710 pounds sterling ($34,586).

But the court found no evidence that Aksoy was murdered by the state after complaining to Strasbourg about his treatment while he was held incommunicado for at least two weeks at the Kiziltepe security prison in southeast Turkey in late 1992.

Aksoy, who complained to the European authorities in May 1993, was found murdered in April 1994. Two days before his death, he received a telephoned warning that he would be killed unless he withdrew his complaint, according to his lawyers.
Turkey told the court a member of the separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) had been charged with the murder.

Though never charged, Askoy said he was subjected to a form of torture known as "Palestinian hanging" in which he was stripped naked and hung by his arms, causing him to lose the use of his arms and hands.
He was also given electric shocks to his genitals, kicked, slapped and verbally abused, he said.
Turkey said the allegations were completely unfounded.
